nodes.name: Point-set distance and Hausdorff distance
nodes.statement:
The distance between a point $\mathbf{x}$ and a set $\mathcal{A}$ in an Euclidean space is defined as $\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{A}) = \inf \{\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\| : \mathbf{y}\in \mathcal{A}\}$, and 
the Hausdorff distance between two sets $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}$ 
is defined by $\mathbf{d}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) = \sup\{ \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{B}) : \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{A}\}$.

nodes.name: Adding the ball constraint without loss of generality
nodes.statement:
In this paper, we aim to determine the asymptotic convergence rate of the moment-SOS hierarchy for a compact semi-algebraic set $\mathcal{X}$. Since $\mathcal{X}$ is bounded, there exists a constant $R$ such that the ball $\mathbb{B}_R$ (with radius $R$ and center at the origin) contains $\mathcal{X}$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $R- \|\mathbf{x}\|^2$ is positive over $\mathcal{X}$. The Schm\"udgen Positivstellensatz theorem implies that there exists a positive integer $t$ such that $R- \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 \in \mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X})_{2t}$. Therefore, if we set $\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}')_{2r}$ to be the preordering of order $2r$ of $\mathcal{X}$ 
    with the additional constraint $R- \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 \geq 0$, then we have 
\begin{displaymath}
     \mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}')_{2r}\subset \mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X})_{2r+2t} \quad \forall\; r \in \mathbb{N}.
\end{displaymath}
This means that the asymptotic convergence rates of $\mathrm{mlb}(f,\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}))_r$ and $\mathrm{lb}(f,\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}))_r$ are equal to that of $\mathrm{mlb}(f,\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}'))_r$ and $\mathrm{lb}(f,\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}'))_r$, respectively. Therefore, without loss of generality,
throughout this paper, most results will be stated under the assumption that the ball constraint $R^2 - \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 \geq 0$ for some suitable $R$ is added to the description~\eqref{domain X} of $\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: Hausdorff distance controls the hierarchy error
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a compact semi-algebraic set and $k \geq {\rm deg}(f)$. Then the errors of the $r$-level of the moment hierarchies are bounded proportionally to the Hausdorff distances as follows:
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        \qquad f_{\min} - \mathrm{mlb}(f,\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}))_r &\leq& \|f\|_1\,\mathbf{d}_k(\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X})_{2r}),\\
        \qquad f_{\min} - \mathrm{mlb}(f,\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X}))_r &\leq&\|f\|_1\,\mathbf{d}_k(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X})_{2r}),\\
        \qquad f_{\min} - \mathrm{mlb}(f,\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{X}))_r &\leq&\|f\|_1\,\mathbf{d}_k(\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{X})_{2r}).
    \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Compactness of pseudo-moment sets and the radius gamma(R,n,k)
nodes.statement:
From now on, we will frequently use the parameter $\gamma(R,n,k)$, where $n$ denotes the dimension of variable $\mathbf{x}$, $k$ denotes the truncation order of the moment sequences, and $R$ is the radius such that $\mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{B}_R$. Since we assume that the inequality $R- \|\mathbf{x}\|^2\geq 0$ is included in the description of $\mathcal{X}$, therefore for any positive even integer $k=2l$, we always have 
    $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X})_k) \subset \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R)_k)$.
    Thus, $\gamma(R,n,k)$ can be used to bound the Euclidean norm of the pseudo-moment sequences in $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X})_k)$.
    The explicit expression of $\gamma(R,n,k)$ is given in 
    the following lemma.
    \begin{lemma}[\cite{josz2016strong}, Lemma 3] For $k=2l,$
        $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R)_k)$ is contained in the Euclidean ball 
        centered at the origin with radius 
        \begin{displaymath}
            \gamma(R,n,k):=\sqrt{\binom{n+l}{n}}\sum_{i=0}^lR^{2i}\,.
        \end{displaymath}
    \end{lemma}

nodes.name: Two-projection plan
nodes.statement:
We prove the theorem by evaluating the distance between an arbitrary pseudo-moment sequence $\mathit{y} \in \mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X})_{2r})$ and $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X})$. First, we conduct two consecutive projections as follows: since $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X}) \subset \mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{Y})$,
we first project $\mathit{y}$ onto $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{Y})$ and denote its projection by $\overline{\mathit{y}}$. By Tchakaloff's theorem, $\overline{\mathit{y}}$ can be written as a convex combination of some $\mathbf{v}_k(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_j)'$s with points $\{\overline{\mathbf{x}}_j : j\in[N]\} \subset \mathcal{Y}$. We continue projecting $\overline{\mathbf{x}}_j$ onto $\mathcal{X}$ to define a new moment sequence $\widetilde{\mathit{y}} \in \mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X})$. These projections are demonstrated in Figure~\ref{Fig: projection with real algebraic variety} and elaborated in the later part of the proof. Then we can upper bound the distance of $\mathit{y}$ to $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X})$ by 
the triangle inequality: 
\begin{equation} \mathbf{d}(\mathit{y},\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X})) \;\leq\; \|\mathit{y} - \widetilde{\mathit{y}}\| \;\leq\; \|\mathit{y}-\overline{\mathit{y}}\| + \|\overline{\mathit{y}}-\widetilde{\mathit{y}}\|.
\end{equation}
The idea of upper-bounding $\mathbf{d}(\mathit{y},\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X}))$ by $\|\mathit{y}-\overline{\mathit{y}}\|$ and $\|\overline{\mathit{y}}-\widetilde{\mathit{y}}\|$ is based on the fact that we already have Theorem~\ref{thm: error on product of simple sets} and the Łojasiewicz inequality~\eqref{Lojaciewicz inequality} as tools to evaluate these terms, which is elaborated next.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement:
We show that the constraint $\widehat{p}_0(\mathbf{z}) :=R+ mK^2 - \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 - \sum_{j=1}^m u_j^2 \geq 0$ can be added to the description of $\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m$ without changing $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r})$.
     Indeed, we can write
     \begin{multline*}
         K^2 - u_j^2= (K-u_j)(K+u_j)= \Bigl(K-\sum_{l=1}^m u_l +\sum_{l \neq j}u_l\Bigr)(K+u_j)
         \\
         = K\Bigl(K-\sum_{l=1}^m u_l\Bigr)+u_j\Bigl(K-\sum_{l=1}^m u_l\Bigr) 
         + K \sum_{l\neq j} u_l + \sum_{l\neq j} u_l u_j \in 
         
         \mathcal{T}\big((\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r}\big)
         \quad \forall j \in [m].
     \end{multline*}
     This implies that we can write $\widehat{p}_0$ as a sum of elements of $\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r}$ of degree at most $2$. In other words, for any product polynomial $q$ of $p_0,\; p_j,\; j \in [m+1]$ with degree at most $2t$ and $\mathit{y} \in \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r})$, we have 
     \begin{eqnarray*}
         &&\widehat{p}_0q = p_0q+\sum_{j=1}^m\Biggl[K\Bigl(K-\sum_{l=1}^m  
         u_l\Bigr)+u_j\Bigl(K-\sum_{l=1}^m u_l\Bigr) 
         + K \sum_{l \neq j}u_l
         + \sum_{l\neq j}u_lu_j
         \Bigr]q
         \\
         &\Rightarrow&\; \mathbf{M}_{r-t-1}(\widehat{p}_0q\mathit{y})
         = \mathbf{M}_{r-t-1}(p_0q\mathit{y})+\sum_{j=1}^mK\mathbf{M}_{r-t-1}\Biggl(\Bigl(K-\sum_{l=1}^m
         u_l\Bigr)q\mathit{y}\Biggr)\\
         &&\qquad +\mathbf{M}_{r-t-1}\Biggl(u_j\Bigl(K-\sum_{l=1}^m u_l\Bigr)q\mathit{y}\Biggr) +\sum_{l \neq j} K \mathbf{M}_{r-t-1} (u_l qy) 
         + \sum_{l\neq j} \mathbf{M}_{r-t-1}\Biggl(u_l u_jq\mathit{y}\Biggr) \succeq 0.
     \end{eqnarray*}
     If we add $\widehat{p}_0(\mathbf{z}) \geq 0$ into the description of $\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m$, the new constraint added to $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r})$
     
     then take the form of 
     \begin{equation*}
         \mathbf{M}_{r-t-1}(\widehat{p}_0q\mathit{y}) \succeq 0.
     \end{equation*}
     However, as we have shown above, the constraint is already satisfied without adding $\widehat{p}_0(\mathbf{z}) \geq 0$. Thus, adding it does not change 
     $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r})$. Furthermore, applying Lemma~\ref{lemm: radius of preordering} gives us that $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r})$ is a compact set contained in the Euclidean ball centered at the origin with radius $\gamma(n+m,R+mK^2,k)$. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm: error on product of simple sets} for the product of two simple sets, we obtain that
     \begin{equation*}
         \mathbf{d}_k(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r}) \leq \Gamma(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m,k)\dfrac{2\gamma(n+m,R+mK^2,k)}{(r-2)^2},
     \end{equation*}
     which is the upper bound we desire. 
 
  Notice that $\varphi(\mathcal{X}) \subset \mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m$, and both $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{T}(\varphi(\mathcal{X}))_{2r})$ and $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{R}(\varphi(\mathcal{X}))_{2r})$ are closed subsets of $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m)_{2r})$. Hence, we can claim that these sets are also compact.

nodes.name: Claim: reformulation
nodes.statement:
The inner product $\langle \cdot,\cdot \rangle_y$ possesses the following properties stated in the book\cite{lasserre2009moments}:
    \begin{align*}
        &\langle q_1,q_2q_3 \rangle_{\mathit{y}} = \langle q_1q_2,q_3 \rangle_{\mathit{y}} \quad \forall q_1, q_2, q_3 \in \mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}],\; {\rm deg} (q_1) + {\rm deg} (q_2) \leq r,\; {\rm deg} (q_2) + {\rm deg} (q_3) \leq r;\\
        & \langle p, g_Jq\rangle_{\mathit{y}} = \mathbf{p}^{\top} \mathbf{M}_{r-\lceil g_J \rceil}(g_J y)\mathbf{q} \quad \forall\; p, q \in 
        \mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{r-\degg{g_J}}.
    \end{align*}
    Therefore, proving the positive semidefiniteness of 
    $\mathbf{M}_{r-\lceil g_J \rceil}(g_J\mathit{y})$ is equivalent to proving that 
    \begin{equation} \langle p, g_Jq\rangle_{\mathit{y}} = \langle p, {g_{m+1}} g_{J^\prime}q\rangle_{\mathit{y}} \;\geq\; 0 \quad \forall\; p, q \in \mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{r-\lceil g_J \rceil}.
    \end{equation}
    In what follows, we prove \eqref{eq sdp} by considering the form of $g_{m+1}$.

nodes.name: Case 1: even monomial
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Case 1: $\widehat{g}(\mathbf{x})= \mathbf{x}^{2\alpha}$.}  For any $i \in [n]$ and $ q \in \mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{r-\lceil g_{J^\prime} \rceil-1}$, we have
\begin{align} &\langle q, (R^2-x_i^2)g_{J^\prime}q\rangle_{\mathit{y}} = \Biggl\langle q, \Bigl(R^2-\sum_{j=1}^nx_j^2\Bigr)g_{J^\prime}q\Biggr \rangle_{\mathit{y}} +\sum_{j \neq i}\langle q, x_j^2g_{J^\prime}q\rangle_{\mathit{y}}\nonumber\\
    =\;& \mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{r-\lceil g_{J^\prime} \rceil-1}\Biggl( \Bigl(R^2-\sum_{j=1}^nx_j^2\Bigr)g_{J^\prime} \mathit{y}\Biggr)\mathbf{q} + \sum_{j \neq i}\langle x_jq,g_{J^\prime}x_jq\rangle_{\mathit{y}}\nonumber\\
    =\;& \mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{r-\lceil g_{J^\prime} \rceil-1}\Biggl( \Bigl(R^2-\sum_{j=1}^nx_j^2\Bigr)g_{J^\prime} \mathit{y}\Biggr)\mathbf{q} + \sum_{j \neq i}\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_j^{\top}\mathbf{M}_{r-\lceil g_{J^\prime} \rceil}( g_{J^\prime} \mathit{y})\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_j \geq 0 \nonumber \\
    \Rightarrow\;& \langle q, x_i^2g_{J^\prime}q\rangle_{\mathit{y}} \leq R^2\langle q, g_{J^\prime}q\rangle_{\mathit{y}}.
\end{align}
In the third equality above, $\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_j$ denotes the vector of coefficients of $x_jq(\mathbf{x})$. The last inequality is based on the positive semidefiniteness of the matrices $\mathbf{M}_{r-\lceil g_{J^\prime} \rceil-1}\big( \big(R^2-\sum_{j=1}^nx_j^2\big)g_{J^\prime} \mathit{y}\big)$ and $\mathbf{M}_{r-\lceil g_{J^\prime} \rceil}( g_{J^\prime} \mathit{y})$. 
Now, for any index $i$ such that $\alpha_i \neq 0$, we can apply \eqref{eq-local} to obtain 
\begin{eqnarray*}
    &\left \langle q, \mathbf{x}^{2\alpha}g_{J^\prime}q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}} = \Bigl \langle qx_i^{\alpha_i-1}\prod_{j \neq i}^nx_j^{\alpha_j}, x_i^2g_{J^\prime}qx_i^{\alpha_i-1}\prod_{j \neq i}^nx_j^{\alpha_j} \Bigr \rangle_{\mathit{y}} \leq R^2\Bigl \langle q,x_i^{2\alpha_i-2}\prod_{j\neq i}^nx_j^{2\alpha_j}g_{J^\prime}q \Bigr \rangle_{\mathit{y}}. 
\end{eqnarray*}
By  repeating the above process for the non-zero components of $\alpha$,
we get 
$$\left \langle q, \mathbf{x}^{2\alpha}g_{J^\prime}q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}}
\leq R^{2|\alpha|}\left \langle q, g_{J^\prime}q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}} \ \forall\; q \in \mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{r-\lceil g_{J^\prime} \rceil-|\alpha|}.
$$

nodes.name: Case 2: signed monomial
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Case 2: $\widehat{g}(\mathbf{x})= \pm\mathbf{x}^{\alpha}$.} We construct $\alpha^{(1)}$ and $\alpha^{(2)}$ as follows: without loss of generality, we assume that there is an index $j$ such that $\alpha_i$ is even for all $i >j$ and $\alpha_i$ is odd for all $i\leq j$. 
Then we set $ \alpha^{(1)}_i=\alpha^{(2)}_i =\alpha_ i $ for $i>j$. 
For index $i \leq j$, we set 
$\alpha^{(1)}_i=\alpha_i+(-1)^i$ and $\alpha^{(2)}_i=\alpha_i-(-1)^i$. Thus, we have  
$\alpha^{(1)} = 2\beta^{(1)}$, $\alpha^{(2)} = 2\beta^{(2)}$
with $\beta^{(1)},\beta^{(2)} \in \mathbb{N}^n_r$ and $\alpha = \beta^{(1)}+\beta^{(2)}$.
By using the identity 
$(\mathbf{x}^{\beta^{(1)}} \pm \mathbf{x}^{\beta^{(2)}})^2 = 
\mathbf{x}^{2\beta^{(1)}} + \mathbf{x}^{2\beta^{(2)}} \pm  2\mathbf{x}^{\alpha} $,
we have that
\begin{eqnarray*}
\Bigl\langle q, (\mathbf{x}^{2\beta^{(1)}} + \mathbf{x}^{2\beta^{(2)}} \pm  2\mathbf{x}^{\alpha})g_{J^\prime}  q\Bigr\rangle \;=\; 
\Bigl\langle (\mathbf{x}^{\beta^{(1)}} \pm \mathbf{x}^{\beta^{(2)}}) q, g_{J^\prime} (\mathbf{x}^{\beta^{(1)}} \pm \mathbf{x}^{\beta^{(2)}}) q\Bigr\rangle_y\; \geq\; 0.
\end{eqnarray*}
Recall that $R \geq 1$. Then we have 
\begin{align*}
   &2 \left \langle q, \pm \mathbf{x}^{\alpha}g_{J^\prime} q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}} \leq \left \langle q, \mathbf{x}^{2\beta^{(1)}}g_{J^\prime} q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}}+ \left \langle q, \mathbf{x}^{2\beta^{(2)}}g_{J^\prime} q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}} \leq 2R^{2\lceil |\alpha|/2\rceil} \left \langle q, g_{J^\prime} q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}}\\
   \Rightarrow\; & \left \langle q, \pm \mathbf{x}^{\alpha}g_{J^\prime} q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}} \leq R^{2\lceil |\alpha|/2\rceil} \left \langle q, g_{J^\prime} q \right \rangle_{\mathit{y}}.
\end{align*}

nodes.statement:
We only prove the first property since the others can
be proved similarly. 
    We first consider the case $k=2r$. In this case,

        \mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta^m_K)_{2r})= \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta^m_K)_{2r}). \quad

Hence, we obtain

    projection of $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{B}_R)_{2r})$,

Let $\mathit{y} \in \mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X})_{2r})$ be an arbitrary truncated pseudo-moment sequence. We proceed to bound the distance from $\mathit{y}$ to $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X})$ by finding an appropriate point $\widetilde{\mathit{y}} \in \mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X})$ and a point $\overline{\mathit{y}} \in \mathcal{M}_k(\mathbb{B}_R)$ such that

     The idea of finding $\overline{\mathit{y}}$ and $\widetilde{\mathit{y}}$ is through lifting $\mathcal{M}_k(\mathcal{X})$ to $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}(\varphi(\mathcal{X}))_{2r})$, where $ \varphi(\mathcal{X})$ is the intersection of a real variety and the product $\mathbb{B}_R \times \Delta_K^m$ of simple sets.

     obtain the desired points $\overline{y}$ and $\widetilde{y}$ by the 
     projection $\psi_k$ defined as in Lemma~\ref{lem: projection into lows dimension}.

         \;=\; \varphi_{2r} \circ \overline{A}_{2r}(\mathbf{x}^{\alpha})
        \;=\; \varphi_{2r} ( (A\mathbf{x})^\alpha)
         \;=\; [\overline{A}_{2r}] e_{\alpha}
     \end{align*}

     So $[\overline{A}_{2r}]$ is also the representation matrix of $\mathcal{A}_{2r}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{s(n,2r)}$ with respect to the standard basis.

Then $\Lambda(\mathcal{X},k)$ depends polynomially on $k$ (for fixed $\mathcal{X}$) and polynomially on $(n_1,\dots,n_m)$ (for fixed $k$).

nodes.name: Polynomial dependence
nodes.statement: We recall from the works \cite{slot2111sum} and \cite{laurent2023effective} that $\tau(\mathcal{X}_i,k)$ depends polynomially on $n_i$ for fixed $k$ and polynomially on $k$ for fixed $n_i$. This leads to our required result. We refer to \cite{slot2111sum} and \cite{laurent2023effective} for the explicit bound on each $\tau(\mathcal{X}_i,k)$ that can be used  to derive an explicit bound on $\Lambda(\mathcal{X},k)$ in terms of $k$ and $n_i$'s.
nodes.statement_short: Known bounds on tau give polynomial dependence.
